q: A case owner authorises two invoice versions. Which decision comes first?
options: Hash the largest accessible disk.
Create an identical working copy of every available partition.
Define the source and selection covered by the authority.
Set the final report title before choosing the time window.
explanation: The question and its authorised boundary determine whether a proposed collection is appropriate.

q: What does a stored raw image most directly represent?
options: The bytes supplied for the selected address range.
Every byte ever present on the underlying physical medium.
Every historical physical byte.
A journal of all user actions.
explanation: The source interface and selected extent determine what enters the recorded byte stream.

q: Which record best distinguishes file-level from volume-level acquisition?
options: The cryptographic algorithm named in the final receipt.
The brand of the destination drive used by the examiner.
The original calendar date of the earliest retained file.
How the acquisition selected its input bytes.
explanation: Two items described as logical images may use very different selection methods.

q: Which question is best answered first from a document service revision history?
options: Who personally made the edit?
Which retained version changed the bank-account field?
Which person was sitting at the laptop during the edit?
Which encrypted storage blocks contain the offline cache?
explanation: A revision history can identify retained changes while personal attribution needs other evidence.

q: An image matches a receipt but the wrong volume was selected. What follows?
options: Matching digests establish that the source authority was fulfilled.
The verified stream still represents the wrong scope.
The omitted partition is known.
The full scope was met.
explanation: Integrity of the produced stream cannot establish that the operator selected the intended source.

q: Why might two valid captures from an encrypted laptop differ?
options: A valid bitwise acquisition must always return identical plaintext.
The two digests should match once the source file names match.
All valid captures show plaintext.
They used different views of the stored data.
explanation: An unlocked file interface and underlying encrypted sectors return different representations.

q: What does a matching digest for the master and working copy support?
options: Their compared byte streams agree at verification.
The computer clock was correct during the original invoice edit.
The stored file came from the person named in its metadata.
The source selection included every relevant invoice version.
explanation: A digest comparison addresses byte integrity for specified objects at the time of comparison.

q: A report shows 16,777,216 bytes. Which description is exact?
options: 16 million bytes exactly.
16 million bytes.
16 MiB.
16 MiB of recovered documents.
explanation: One mebibyte is 1,048,576 bytes and the size alone says nothing about content.

q: What extra question does reading the destination again answer?
options: Did the case owner authorise a capture of this particular source?
Was the original invoice edited by its directory account owner?
Did the stored result retain the bytes expected?
Was the collection authorised?
explanation: Reading back the destination tests the stored copy independently of a digest calculated during transfer.

q: A tool reports the first difference at character 100001. Which zero-based offset is that?
options: 99999, because numbering begins one byte before the file.
It cannot be determined even if the numbering conventions are known.
explanation: Converting a one-based position to a zero-based offset requires subtracting one.

q: How should an examiner interpret the changed working-copy digest in the fixture?
options: Treat the preserved master as altered without checking it.
Replace the recorded source digest with the working-copy value.
Replace the expected digest.
Record a discrepancy in that derivative.
explanation: The observed change involves the derivative and does not establish an alteration to the original.

q: Which result identifies the location of the changed byte?
options: The opening characters of the new SHA-256 value.
The separate byte comparison.
The destination name assigned during the acquisition.
The SHA-256 prefix.
explanation: A digest mismatch signals a difference but does not provide its location.

q: A tool substitutes zeros for two unreadable sectors. What must accompany the image?
options: A new checksum only.
The affected addresses and the handling recorded by the tool.
A claim that the entire copy failed despite all other readable regions.
A new expected digest computed only after deleting the acquisition log.
explanation: The stored zero pattern cannot by itself identify which regions the tool could not read.

q: Which statement fits a verified image with two documented unreadable regions?
options: Every address in the source yielded the exact bytes now in storage.
The whole source was recovered.
Every source zero was read.
The stored output verifies, with gaps in source coverage.
explanation: A verified copy of a produced stream can contain documented substitutions for unavailable source bytes.

q: An export contains only the current version. Which report wording is justified?
options: The supplied export contains no earlier version.
No previous version existed anywhere in the organisation.
The previous version was deliberately deleted by the file owner.
The local synchronisation client never stored an earlier version.
explanation: The result describes the observed selection and does not establish the history of other sources.

q: Why retain an acquisition log when the output has a digest?
options: It reconstructs lost bytes.
The log makes additional scope approval unnecessary for later cases.
The log documents collection decisions and read errors.
The log proves that the assigned user personally edited the invoice.
explanation: The digest records a property of bytes while the log describes how they were obtained.

q: Which timing detail belongs in a defensible receipt?
options: Only the time at which the examiner finished writing the report.
The report completion date only.
Original time values and their time zones.
A single rounded local time.
explanation: Receipt, acquisition and modification are different events that can be recorded on different clocks.

q: The investigator needs evidence outside the authorised boundary. What is the next step?
options: Request authority for the additional source.
Collect it under the old approval because the device is at hand.
Use a separate destination to treat the source as already authorised.
Collect under the old approval.
explanation: A technical opportunity to read more evidence does not expand the documented case authority.

q: The captured directory has no old register. Which follow-up best tests local-only changes?
options: Conclude that the final cloud revision always matches every endpoint.
Identify the author by comparing the directory and file names alone.
Treat the absence of older files as evidence of deliberate deletion.
Check whether an authorised synchronisation history exists.
explanation: A separate record may establish what the selected export cannot show about synchronisation.

q: Two receipts name image.dd. What should a reviewer seek before comparing them?
options: Proof that the base file names are spelled identically on both receipts.
Case identifiers and their links to each source.
The last access dates alone.
The base file names alone.
explanation: Names can repeat across folders or cases, so establish exactly which objects the receipts identify.

q: Which item belongs in the scope description of a volume image?
options: The last person physically present when the evidence was discussed.
The selected volume and its readable address range.
The working directory of the person who later drafted the narrative.
The selected hashing algorithm.
explanation: The address range helps another examiner understand the boundary of the acquired material.

q: A valid source digest and a destination digest differ. What should happen first?
options: Replace the expected digest.
Attribute deliberate tampering to the last person in the custody record.
Discard the master and keep only the working copy that investigators used.
Preserve both results and verify what was compared.
explanation: A mismatch calls for checking source identity, method and custody before drawing conclusions.

q: Why can a live acquisition need a start time and a finish time?
options: Its source can change during the read.
Its end time always reveals the exact moment of every source change.
Its two timestamps remove the need to document errors and exclusions.
It proves the source stayed still.
explanation: A changing source may contribute bytes from different moments in the collection interval.

q: A working copy still matches the expected digest but the stored master does not. Which claim is premature?
options: The master needs a new independent read from its documented location.
The expected digest should be checked against the correct case item.
The stored master was deliberately tampered with.
A fresh read is warranted.
explanation: Mismatch warrants investigation and does not establish deliberate alteration or a responsible individual.

q: Which statement best closes the fictional invoice acquisition decision?
options: The account identifies the editor.
A byte-identical copy removes uncertainty about missing service revisions.
The retained revisions can show a field change within their scope.
The device image can prove every event outside the authorised time period.
explanation: A scoped conclusion connects the evidence to the question while leaving unsupported attribution open.
